scenes.heading: 1. hook (green river, dead fish)
scenes.speech: In late 1991, almost a thousand kilometres of the Barwon and Darling rivers turned green with cyanobacteria. In the summer of 2018 to 2019, near Menindee on the lower Darling, fish deaths were estimated at more than a million. Those deaths were linked to low flow, heat and algal blooms that left the water short of oxygen. So why would extra nutrients end in a fish kill, and what should chemists measure to see it coming?

scenes.heading: 2. nutrients: needed, until there's too much
scenes.speech: Nitrogen and phosphorus aren't poisons. Algae and plants need them to grow. In a lake, growth is usually held back by whichever nutrient is in shortest supply, called the limiting nutrient, and in fresh water that's often phosphorus. Add more of it, and you've taken the brake off.

scenes.heading: 3. where the extra comes from
scenes.speech: So where does the extra come from? After heavy rain, fertiliser washes off paddocks into creeks. That's a diffuse source, spread over a whole catchment. Sewage effluent and drains are point sources, one outlet you can point to, and they bring nutrients and organic waste together. Urban stormwater adds more. The source matters, because it decides where you sample and what the fix is.

scenes.heading: 4. feed and bloom
scenes.speech: With the brake off, algae multiply into a bloom, a green scum you can see from the bank. In daylight, those algae make oxygen as they photosynthesise. At night they use oxygen as they respire, like every living thing in the water. So a bloom can give a high oxygen reading at noon, and a much lower one at dawn.

scenes.heading: 5. die, decay, suffocate
scenes.speech: Then the bloom runs out of something, light or nutrients, and the algae die and sink. Bacteria decompose the dead algae, and as they respire they use up dissolved oxygen, the oxygen gas dissolved in the water. They use it faster than it can dissolve back in from the air, especially in warm, still water. Oxygen falls, and fish suffocate. So the algae don't kill the fish directly. The worst comes days after the bloom, which is why the danger is easy to miss.

scenes.heading: 6. a name and a memory aid
scenes.speech: This chain is called eutrophication: nutrients enrich the water, too much grows, and the oxygen crashes. Five words carry it. Feed, bloom, die, decay, suffocate. And remember why the crash is worse in summer. Warm water holds less oxygen, the way a warm soft drink goes flat.

scenes.heading: 7. one look isn't enough
scenes.speech: So how would you see this coming? Not by looking. Clear water can still carry dissolved nutrients, salts or metals, and a pH of seven says nothing about oxygen. Water quality is a set of measurements, read together. Chemists group them as physical, chemical and biological.

scenes.heading: 8. physical
scenes.speech: Physical parameters come first. Temperature matters because warm water holds less oxygen. Turbidity is cloudiness from suspended particles. Cloudy water blocks light and often means soil has washed in, but turbidity can't tell you about dissolved poisons or germs.

scenes.heading: 9. chemical
scenes.speech: Chemical parameters include pH, dissolved oxygen and conductivity. Conductivity rises with dissolved ions, so it's a quick check for salts, but it can't say which ions are there. For nitrate and phosphate, a reagent turns each one into a coloured compound, read against standards just like in the last video. Or ion chromatography separates the ions in a column and measures each one as it comes out.

scenes.heading: 10. biological
scenes.speech: Biological parameters look at living things. E. coli are gut bacteria, so finding them in water means faecal contamination, from sewage or animals. Counting algal cells under a microscope shows a bloom starting before you can see it from the bank.

scenes.heading: 11. worked read: which site is further along?
scenes.speech: Let's read some data. Three sites on a lake, measured on the same day. Read one column at a time. Nitrate and phosphate rise from A to C, and site B already has about nine times the phosphate of A. Dissolved oxygen falls from eight point four to three point nine milligrams per litre. And the observations agree: clear water, then scum, then dead fish. So C is furthest along, and B is heading the same way. What the table can't show is what the oxygen does at night.

scenes.heading: 12. why monitor?
scenes.speech: So why monitor? A number only means something against a guideline for that water's use. For drinking water, the nitrate guideline is fifty milligrams per litre, set to protect babies, but far lower nutrient levels can feed a bloom in a river. Sampling above and below a source finds where the nutrients enter, and that decides the fix. Monitoring also tells a treatment plant what it has to remove, like algae at a drinking water intake, or nitrogen and phosphorus in sewage before it's released. And after any fix, only measurement shows whether the water recovered.

scenes.heading: 13. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Your turn. A creek flows past a dairy farm, and water is sampled at three sites. Use the data to identify the most likely source of the nutrients. Then explain why dissolved oxygen is lowest at site three, not site two. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 14. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.speech: Nitrate, phosphate and E. coli all jump between sites one and two, so the dairy drain is the source, and the E. coli points to animal waste. Oxygen is lowest at site three because a bloom needs time. In that slow pool, algae grew, died and decayed, and bacteria used the oxygen. Expecting the lowest oxygen where nutrients are highest is the trap.

scenes.heading: 15. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Last one. A water authority wants early warning that a drinking water dam is heading toward an algal bloom. Choose one physical, one chemical and one biological parameter, and explain what each would show. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 16. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.speech: One good set: water temperature, because warm, still water favours blooms. Phosphate and nitrate, because rising nutrients come before the bloom. And algal cell counts, to catch the bloom starting. Counting dead fish isn't a warning. It shows the crash has already happened.

scenes.heading: 17. handoff
scenes.speech: So, when you're asked why we monitor water, trace it from the source, through the bloom, to the oxygen crash, then choose evidence of all three kinds for the job. Next, how chemists actually measure that oxygen, and the test that forecasts how fast it'll be used up.

scenes.heading: 18. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (first light)
scenes.speech: In March 2023, millions of fish died in the Darling-Baaka River at Menindee. The New South Wales Chief Scientist's review found that low dissolved oxygen was the most likely cause, and the biggest die-offs came around first light. A reading at noon could have looked fine. So what do dissolved oxygen and BOD tell us, and how do chemists measure them?

scenes.heading: 2. dissolved oxygen
scenes.speech: Dissolved oxygen, or DO, is the oxygen gas dissolved in the water, measured in milligrams per litre. Fish and other water animals breathe it through their gills. Fresh water at twenty degrees can hold only about nine milligrams per litre, and warmer water holds less. When DO falls to just a few milligrams per litre, many fish struggle.

scenes.heading: 3. a snapshot
scenes.speech: But DO changes through the day. In a lake full of algae it can be high in the afternoon and lowest at dawn, so one reading is a snapshot. A DO meter puts a probe straight into the water, gives a reading in seconds, and can log all night. Meters drift, though, so they're calibrated and checked against a chemical method, the Winkler titration.

scenes.heading: 4. taking the sample
scenes.speech: The Winkler method starts at the river. The bottle is filled to overflowing, with no air bubbles, and stoppered. That matters, because air contains oxygen, and a single bubble would add some. Then the oxygen is fixed straight away, so it can't escape or change.

scenes.heading: 5. step 1: fix the oxygen
scenes.speech: Step one. Add manganese two sulfate, then an alkaline iodide solution. A pale manganese two hydroxide forms, and the dissolved oxygen oxidises it straight away to a brown solid. Every oxygen molecule in the bottle is now locked up in that brown solid, and nothing can get in or out.

scenes.heading: 6. step 2: turn it into iodine
scenes.speech: Step two. Add sulfuric acid. The brown solid dissolves, and its manganese is now strong enough to oxidise iodide ions to iodine. The solution turns yellow-brown. The more oxygen there was, the more brown solid formed, and the more iodine you get.

scenes.heading: 7. step 3: titrate the iodine
scenes.speech: Step three. A measured portion goes into a flask, and sodium thiosulfate from a burette turns the iodine back into iodide. As the yellow fades to pale straw, add a little starch. It turns blue-black with iodine, and the endpoint is the moment the blue disappears. So thiosulfate never meets the oxygen itself. It measures the iodine, and the iodine stands in for the oxygen.

scenes.heading: 8. the ratio, step by step
scenes.speech: So how much thiosulfate per oxygen? Follow the equations. One oxygen molecule fixes two manganese. Each manganese frees one iodine, so that's two iodine. And each iodine takes two thiosulfates, so four thiosulfates in all. One oxygen, four thiosulfates.

scenes.heading: 9. worked example: moles of thiosulfate
scenes.speech: Let's work one. A hundred millilitre sample needs eight point zero zero millilitres of point zero one zero zero molar thiosulfate. Find the dissolved oxygen in milligrams per litre. Start with the solution you know both numbers for. Moles equals c times V: point zero one zero zero times point zero zero eight zero zero litres is eight point zero zero times ten to the minus five moles of thiosulfate.

scenes.heading: 10. worked example: ratio, then mass
scenes.speech: Now use the ratio. Divide by four: two point zero zero times ten to the minus five moles of oxygen. Times thirty two gives six point four zero times ten to the minus four grams, which is point six four zero milligrams, all in that hundred millilitre sample.

scenes.heading: 11. worked example: per litre
scenes.speech: We want milligrams per litre, so divide by the sample's volume in litres, not by the titre. Point six four zero over point one zero zero zero is six point four zero milligrams per litre. Water at twenty degrees can hold about nine, so if this sample was at twenty degrees, it's about seventy per cent full.

scenes.heading: 12. BOD: the forecast
scenes.speech: DO tells you the oxygen now. Biochemical oxygen demand, or BOD, forecasts how fast it'll be used. Fill two bottles from the same sample. Measure the DO in one straight away. Seal the other and keep it in the dark at twenty degrees for five days. Sealed, so no new oxygen gets in. Dark, so algae can't make oxygen. Twenty degrees, so every lab's results compare. Then measure it again. The oxygen that's gone was used by microbes breaking down organic matter. So a high BOD means lots of oxygen used, not lots of oxygen present.

scenes.heading: 13. worked BOD and what it means
scenes.speech: So BOD five is the starting DO minus the DO after five days. A sample starts at eight point four, and after five days it's down to four point nine. That's a BOD of three point five milligrams per litre. Microbes in each litre used three point five milligrams of oxygen in five days, moderate on the guide many courses use.

scenes.heading: 14. reading DO and BOD together, and BOD's limits
scenes.speech: Read the two together. Low DO with a high BOD means the water is short of oxygen and still losing it, which is the pattern before a fish kill. But BOD only sees what microbes can break down. Metals, pesticides and germs don't show up, and a poison can even stop the microbes, so the BOD reads low. A low BOD doesn't prove water is safe. And it takes five days, so for tonight, you still need the probe.

scenes.heading: 15. memory aid
scenes.speech: Two lines to keep. DO is oxygen now. BOD is oxygen used later. And for the Winkler calculation, one oxygen, four thiosulfates.

scenes.heading: 16. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Your turn. A fifty millilitre river sample is analysed by the Winkler method, and the iodine needs ten point four zero millilitres of point zero zero five zero zero molar thiosulfate. Calculate the dissolved oxygen in milligrams per litre. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 17. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.speech: Moles of thiosulfate, c times V, is five point two zero times ten to the minus five. Divide by four for oxygen, then times thirty two: point four one six milligrams in fifty millilitres. That's eight point three two milligrams per litre. Using one to one gives thirty three, more oxygen than water can hold.

scenes.heading: 18. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Last one. Creek water is sampled above and below a food-processing plant's outlet, and each sample is tested for BOD. Calculate the BOD five of each sample, then explain what the result below the outlet suggests about the creek downstream. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 19. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.speech: P's BOD is point nine, and Q's is five point eight milligrams per litre. Q carries much more organic waste, so microbes will keep using oxygen as the water flows on, and DO downstream is likely to fall, especially on warm nights. Calling Q's BOD one point eight is the trap. That's the oxygen left, not the oxygen used.

scenes.heading: 20. handoff
scenes.speech: So DO is the oxygen in the water right now, and BOD is how fast it's being used up. Read them together, and remember what neither can see. Next, Module 8 turns to organic compounds, and the simple tests that tell their functional groups apart.

scenes.heading: 21. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (five bottles, no labels)
scenes.speech: Five bottles on the prep room bench have lost their labels. The list says they hold cyclohexane, cyclohexene, ethanol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol and ethanoic acid. They're all colourless liquids, so looking won't help. You can't see a double bond or an O H group, but you can see what it does. Three quick tests, each watching for one group, can rule candidates out.

scenes.heading: 2. a test is a reaction you can see
scenes.speech: Each test borrows a reaction from Module 7. The trick is to pick a reaction that only one of these groups does quickly, with a change you can see: a colour that goes, a colour that changes, or a gas that fizzes. So before you test, predict. Which group adds bromine? Which group is acidic enough to react with a carbonate? And which group can be oxidised?

scenes.heading: 3. C=C: the fade
scenes.speech: First, the carbon to carbon double bond. Add a few drops of orange bromine water and shake. Bromine adds across the double bond and gets used up, so the orange colour fades within seconds. You ran this test in the bromine water practical. An alkane has no double bond to open, so it stays orange. On our list, cyclohexene fades it and cyclohexane doesn't. Bright light lets an alkane react slowly, so test in normal room light and read it at once.

scenes.heading: 4. –COOH: the fizz
scenes.speech: Next, the carboxylic acid. Add sodium hydrogen carbonate. A carboxylic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, so it gives the hydrogen carbonate a proton. The carbonic acid breaks up into water and carbon dioxide, and the tube fizzes. Bubble that gas through limewater, and it turns milky, which confirms carbon dioxide. An alcohol is far too weak an acid to do this, so it doesn't fizz.

scenes.heading: 5. –OH: the green
scenes.speech: Then the hydroxyl group. Warm the sample with acidified potassium dichromate. A primary or secondary alcohol is oxidised, and the orange dichromate ions are reduced to green chromium three ions. Ethanol is a primary alcohol, so it turns green. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on its O H carbon, so it stays orange. Hydrocarbons and ethanoic acid usually leave it orange too. Esterification is a second hydroxyl test, but it relies on judging a smell, so here dichromate does the work.

scenes.heading: 6. what green can and can't say
scenes.speech: Green tells you something in the tube was oxidised. Aldehydes do that too, so green points to a primary or secondary alcohol only when aldehydes aren't among the candidates. On our list, they aren't. And orange doesn't prove there's no O H group. A tertiary alcohol has one, and stays orange anyway. So orange means no primary or secondary alcohol was detected.

scenes.heading: 7. fresh portions, and the order
scenes.speech: Use a fresh portion of the sample for each test, so one reagent can't spoil the next result. Then the order doesn't change any result. It changes how much hazard you face. Start with the mildest reagent, sodium hydrogen carbonate, then bromine water. Dichromate contains chromium six, so it comes last, as a teacher demonstration in a fume cupboard.

scenes.heading: 8. one molecule, two groups
scenes.speech: Here's the trap. A yes for one group doesn't mean no for the others. Prop-2-en-1-ol has a double bond and an O H group. It fades bromine water, so it looks like an alkene. But it also turns dichromate green. If you stopped at the first yes, you'd miss the alcohol. In the same way, an acid with a double bond would fizz and fade. So run all three tests, and report each group on its own.

scenes.heading: 9. excluding candidates
scenes.speech: Back to the bench. One bottle gives no fizz, so ethanoic acid is out. Bromine water stays orange, so cyclohexene is out. Dichromate turns green, so cyclohexane and the tertiary alcohol are out, because both would stay orange. Only ethanol fits all three results. Notice that the no results did half the work, so write down every result, even when nothing happens. Every no rules a candidate out.

scenes.heading: 10. what the tests can't tell you
scenes.speech: Suppose another bottle had given no change in all three tests. That fits cyclohexane, and it fits 2-methylpropan-2-ol, so these tests can't separate them. You'd need different evidence, like an infrared spectrum, which shows an O H band. They also can't say whether an alcohol is primary or secondary, or where a double bond sits. They show which groups are present, not the whole structure. For that, you'll use the spectra coming up in this module.

scenes.heading: 11. memory aid
scenes.speech: One line for the three tests: fizz, fade, green. Fizz for a carboxylic acid, fade for a double bond, green for a primary or secondary alcohol. Run all three, each on a fresh portion.

scenes.heading: 12. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Your turn. An unknown is one of the four compounds on the card. It gives no fizz with sodium hydrogen carbonate, it decolourises bromine water within seconds, and it turns acidified dichromate green. Identify the unknown, and justify your answer. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 13. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.speech: No fizz rules out hexanoic acid. The fading bromine water shows a double bond, which rules out hexan-1-ol. The green dichromate shows a primary or secondary alcohol, which hex-1-ene doesn't have. Only hex-5-en-1-ol has both. Picking hex-1-ene after the bromine result is the slip: one yes doesn't rule out the others.

scenes.heading: 14. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Last one. Liquid Q gives no fizz with sodium hydrogen carbonate, and a student concludes that Q is an alcohol. Evaluate this conclusion, and outline two further tests that would show which groups Q contains. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 15. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.speech: The conclusion isn't supported. No fizz only rules out a carboxylic acid, so Q could still be an alkane, an alkene or an alcohol. Test a fresh portion with bromine water: a fade shows a double bond. Warm another with acidified dichromate: green supports a primary or secondary alcohol, but a tertiary alcohol would stay orange. Treating one no as a yes for something else is the trap.

scenes.heading: 16. decision rule and handoff
scenes.speech: So, when you meet an unknown, ask three questions. Does it fizz, does bromine water fade, does dichromate turn green? Answer each on a fresh portion, let every no rule candidates out, and report each group the results support. Next, the practical: running these tests safely, with the right controls.

scenes.heading: 17. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (four bottles, four claims)
scenes.speech: Four bottles, A to D, each hold one unknown organic liquid. Your job isn't to name them. It's to say which functional groups your results support, and which ones they can't rule out. That takes three tests, the right controls beside each one, and a safe plan for the one reagent that contains chromium six.

scenes.heading: 2. the aim and the plan
scenes.speech: The aim: to test unknown organic liquids for a carbon to carbon double bond, a hydroxyl group and a carboxylic acid group. Your teacher tells you each unknown is a hydrocarbon, an alcohol or a carboxylic acid. Each unknown gets three tests, each on a fresh portion. You run the fizz test and the bromine water test. The dichromate test is a teacher demonstration. The independent variable is which liquid is in the tube, and the dependent variable is what you see.

scenes.heading: 3. blank and known
scenes.speech: Every test needs two controls beside the unknown. A blank uses distilled water instead of a sample. It should show no change, so if the blank does change, something else caused it: the tube, the water or the reagent. A known uses a liquid that has the group, like ethanoic acid for the fizz test. It shows the reagent works today, and what a positive looks like. So every row reads blank, known, unknown.

scenes.heading: 4. bromine water: the p02 method
scenes.speech: You've already run the bromine water test, so use the same method. One millilitre of sample to two millilitres of bromine water, stoppered and shaken for ten seconds, in normal room light, and read at once against a white tile. Cyclohexene is the known, and it fades within seconds. Water is the blank, diluted just as much, and it stays orange.

scenes.heading: 5. the fizz test, and checking the gas
scenes.speech: Put two millilitres of the unknown in a test tube, and add a small spatula of solid sodium hydrogen carbonate. The known, ethanoic acid, fizzes straight away, and the blank doesn't. To check the gas, fit a bung and delivery tube, and bubble the gas through limewater. Carbon dioxide turns it milky. Judge a few bubbles against the known and the blank, not against what you expected.

scenes.heading: 6. the dichromate demonstration
scenes.speech: Now the dichromate test. Your teacher runs it in a fume cupboard, with small volumes: two millilitres of acidified potassium dichromate in each tube, and five drops of liquid. The tubes stand in a water bath at about sixty degrees, with no flame nearby. This batch holds ethanol, the known, then unknowns B and D, and water, the blank. After about five minutes, ethanol and B have turned green. D and the blank stay orange.

scenes.heading: 7. batch two, and what the colours claim
scenes.speech: The teacher runs A and C the same way, with a repeat of D, and all three stay orange. Green shows something was oxidised. There are no aldehydes among the unknowns, so green supports a primary or secondary alcohol. Orange means no primary or secondary alcohol was detected. It doesn't prove there's no O H group, because a tertiary alcohol stays orange too.

scenes.heading: 8. record as you go
scenes.speech: Record as you go, in a table drawn up beforehand. One row per tube: the liquid, the reagent, what you saw, and only then, what it means. Write no visible change in full, never a blank cell, because a negative is evidence too. Record the controls as well. If a blank changed, that row can't be trusted.

scenes.heading: 9. supported, not detected, can't tell
scenes.speech: A fizzed, and its gas turned limewater milky, so a carboxylic acid is supported. C faded the bromine water, so a double bond is supported. B turned dichromate green, so a primary or secondary alcohol is supported. D changed nothing, so nothing was detected, but D could be an alkane or a tertiary alcohol. The teacher's key says D is 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Your claim still holds, because it said only what the tests could show.

scenes.heading: 10. valid, reliable, accurate?
scenes.speech: Now the three words from the skills video. Valid? Each test should respond only to its group, and fresh portions, clean tubes and a blank that stays unchanged protect that. Reliable? Repeat the deciding tests, like D's dichromate tube, and compare with another group. Accurate? Here the result is a claim about groups, so it's accurate when it matches the true structure. The knowns and the teacher's key show how close you got.

scenes.heading: 11. the risk assessment
scenes.speech: Now the risks. Potassium dichromate contains chromium six: it's toxic, can cause cancer, and can trigger allergies. That's why your teacher handles it, in small volumes in a fume cupboard, with gloves and glasses, and chromium residues go into heavy-metal waste. The organic liquids are flammable, so use a water bath, never a flame. Bromine vapour irritates the eyes and lungs, so bromine water stays in the fume cupboard. Never smell an unknown to identify it. Organic residues go into the labelled organic waste, never the sink. Pause if you want to copy the full table.

scenes.heading: 12. memory aid
scenes.speech: One line for your claims: supported, not detected, can't tell. A positive with a clean blank supports a group. A negative means not detected, not absent. And when two answers give the same results, say you can't tell.

scenes.heading: 13. attempt 1 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Your turn. In a demonstration, four test tubes were rinsed with ethanol to help them dry. Acidified dichromate was warmed with water, with ethanol, and with unknowns S and T. All four turned green, and a student concluded that S and T both contain a primary or secondary alcohol. Evaluate this conclusion, and propose an improvement. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 14. feedback 1 (brief)
scenes.speech: Not valid. The water blank turned green, so something other than the samples reduced the dichromate: ethanol left from the rinse. So S and T's results can't be trusted. Rinse clean tubes with distilled water and let them dry, then repeat with a blank that stays orange. Just repeating the test is the trap: the same ethanol turns it green again.

scenes.heading: 15. attempt 2 (countdown, 10 seconds)
scenes.speech: Last one. Unknown E fizzes with sodium hydrogen carbonate, and the gas turns limewater milky. It decolourises bromine water within seconds, and it leaves acidified dichromate orange. Every blank shows no change. State which groups the results support, which were not detected, and one limitation. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 16. feedback 2 (brief)
scenes.speech: The fizz and the milky limewater support a carboxylic acid. The fading bromine water supports a double bond too, because one molecule can carry both. No primary or secondary alcohol was detected, but a tertiary O H can't be ruled out. Calling it an acid and dismissing the bromine result is the slip.

scenes.heading: 17. decision rule and handoff
scenes.speech: So, for any unknown organic liquid: three tests on fresh portions, a blank and a known beside each, observations before inferences, and only the claims your results support. Next: mass spectrometry, which weighs the molecule itself.

scenes.heading: 18. key notes (quiet, hold about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (most changed cells never become cancer)
scenes.speech: Every day, your body makes huge numbers of new cells by mitosis, and each time DNA is copied, a few changes can slip through. So most of us carry cells with changed DNA. Yet most of those cells never become cancer. Why not? And when one does, how does it spread? That's today's question: how does cancer begin and spread?

scenes.heading: 2. cancer is mitosis without control
scenes.speech: Start with what you know. In mitosis, a cell copies its chromosomes, lines them up, separates the copies and splits in two, so each new cell gets a full set. A cancer cell still divides by mitosis. The main problem isn't how it divides, but when. Healthy cells divide when the body needs them, like when a graze heals. A cancer cell keeps dividing when it should stop.

scenes.heading: 3. the cell cycle and its checkpoints
scenes.speech: A cell's life runs in a loop called the cell cycle. It grows, copies its DNA, gets ready, then divides. Along the loop sit checkpoints, stops where the cell checks that it's safe to go on. You've met one: before the copies separate, the cell waits until every chromosome is attached from both ends. Another comes before the DNA is copied. It asks: is the cell big enough, is there a signal to divide, and is the DNA undamaged?

scenes.heading: 4. p53: repair or self-destruct
scenes.speech: At that checkpoint, a protein called p53 checks for DNA damage. If it finds some, it stops the cycle, so repair enzymes can fix it. If the damage is too great, p53 triggers apoptosis: the cell destroys itself in a controlled way, so the fault is never copied. That's the first answer. Most changed cells are repaired, or they remove themselves, before they can divide.

scenes.heading: 5. several changes, one cell line
scenes.speech: So for cancer, the controls themselves have to break, and that usually takes several mutations in the same line of cells. A cell with one change that lets it divide a bit more often leaves more descendants than its neighbours. One of those picks up a second change, and its descendants take over again. That's why it usually takes years, and why cancer becomes more common as people age.

scenes.heading: 6. the accelerator: proto-oncogenes
scenes.speech: Which genes? Two kinds control division. Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that tell a cell to divide when a growth signal arrives. They're the accelerator. A mutation can jam the accelerator down, so the gene's protein says divide even with no signal from outside. The mutated gene is called an oncogene. And one mutated copy is enough, because a protein that's stuck on overrides the normal copy.

scenes.heading: 7. the brakes: tumour suppressor genes
scenes.speech: The other kind are tumour suppressor genes, the brakes. They stop division, repair DNA or trigger apoptosis, and the gene for p53 is one of them. One working copy usually still makes enough brake, so both copies normally have to be lost. That's why inheriting one faulty copy, like a faulty BRCA1 gene, raises the risk of cancer a lot, but doesn't make it certain. So cancer is a stuck accelerator and failed brakes, though real cancers need several such changes.

scenes.heading: 8. melanoma: UV as a named environmental risk
scenes.speech: Now a real case. Australia has some of the world's highest melanoma rates, and UV light from the sun is its main cause. UV damages DNA in melanocytes, the skin cells that make pigment. In many melanomas, one mutation jams an accelerator gene called BRAF, and later mutations knock out brakes. That cell line divides out of control and forms a tumour, a lump of cells that keep dividing.

scenes.heading: 9. benign or malignant
scenes.speech: But tumours aren't all dangerous in the same way. A benign tumour, like most moles, stays where it started. It can grow, but it doesn't invade. A malignant tumour does. Its cells break through a thin sheet under the top layer of skin, called the basement membrane, into the layer below, where blood and lymph vessels run. A way to remember it: malignant moves, benign is bound.

scenes.heading: 10. metastasis, step by step
scenes.speech: Spreading to a new site is called metastasis, and it takes several steps. Cells break away, because they've lost the proteins that stick them to their neighbours. They squeeze into a lymph or blood vessel and get carried off. Most die on the way. A few survive, leave the vessel somewhere else and grow a new, secondary tumour. For melanoma, that's often a nearby lymph node first, then organs such as the lungs, liver or brain.

scenes.heading: 11. why spread matters
scenes.speech: That's why metastasis causes most cancer deaths. Once tumours grow in several organs, they're much harder to remove. It's also why finding melanoma early matters: while it's thin and hasn't reached the vessels, cutting it out usually cures it. And the main cause can be reduced: slip, slop, slap, seek and slide.

scenes.heading: 12a. attempt one (one copy each)
scenes.speech: Two exam questions. First. Cell A has one mutated copy of a proto-oncogene. Cell B has one mutated copy of a tumour suppressor gene. Every other copy is normal. Predict which cell is more likely to divide without a growth signal, and explain your prediction. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 12b. feedback, item one
scenes.speech: Cell A. Its mutation turns the proto-oncogene into an oncogene, whose protein is stuck on, so one copy can drive division with no signal. In cell B, the normal copy of the tumour suppressor gene still makes enough brake, so control usually holds until that copy is lost too. The classic mistake is saying both are equally likely, because each has one mutation.

scenes.heading: 12c. attempt two (HPV and the cervix)
scenes.speech: Second. Some types of human papillomavirus, or HPV, infect cells lining the cervix. One viral protein, called E6, causes the cell to destroy its p53. Explain how this infection can increase the risk of cancer. Then explain why a growth that hasn't crossed the basement membrane is unlikely to have spread. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 12d. feedback, item two
scenes.speech: Without p53, the checkpoint can't stop a damaged cell. It isn't repaired and doesn't destroy itself, so it keeps dividing and copying its mutations, and more can build up in that line. That raises the risk, but not every infection leads to cancer. And to spread, cells must break through the basement membrane to reach vessels. The classic mistake is calling cervical cancer a cancer you catch.

scenes.heading: 13. decision rule and handoff
scenes.speech: So for any cancer question, follow the chain: mutations build up, a control breaks, an accelerator stuck on or a brake lost, then division without stopping, a tumour, and, if it's malignant, invasion and spread. Next, how common is a disease? Incidence, prevalence and mortality.

scenes.heading: 14. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (more deaths, lower chance)
scenes.speech: More Australians die of cancer each year now than thirty years ago. Yet at any given age, your chance of dying of cancer is lower than it was then. Both statements are true. To see how, you need to know exactly what each disease number measures. So today's question: what do incidence, prevalence and mortality measure?

scenes.heading: 2. three measures, three questions
scenes.speech: You've met two of these with dengue. Incidence counts new cases in a set time, and prevalence counts everyone who has the disease at one moment. Incidence is the tap, prevalence is the tank. Now add a third. Mortality counts deaths from the disease in a set time, mort as in mortuary. So it's how many new cases, how many people living with it, and how many deaths.

scenes.heading: 3. a case, a population, a time window
scenes.speech: Every rate needs three things defined. First, what counts as a case, for example a diagnosis confirmed by a doctor. Second, the population at risk: the people who could get the disease. For cervical cancer, that's females, not everyone. Third, the time window: usually a year for incidence and mortality, but a single date for prevalence, because it's a snapshot. Leave any of these vague, and two rates that look alike may not be comparable.

scenes.heading: 4. worked: incidence
scenes.speech: Let's work all three for type 2 diabetes in one city of eighty thousand people. In 2025, a hundred and sixty people were newly diagnosed. For incidence, new cases go on top and the population goes underneath, then we multiply by a hundred thousand. A hundred and sixty divided by eighty thousand is zero point zero zero two. Times a hundred thousand, that's two hundred per hundred thousand per year. Sense check: that's two in every thousand people, which fits.

scenes.heading: 5. worked: prevalence, two ways
scenes.speech: Now prevalence. On the thirtieth of June 2025, four thousand four hundred people in the city were living with type 2 diabetes. These are all existing cases, counted on one day, so there's no "per year". Four thousand four hundred over eighty thousand is zero point zero five five. As a percentage, that's five point five per cent. Per hundred thousand, it's five thousand five hundred. Use whichever form the question asks for, but don't mix them.

scenes.heading: 6. worked: mortality
scenes.speech: Third, mortality. In 2025, sixteen people in the city died from type 2 diabetes. Sixteen over eighty thousand, times a hundred thousand, is twenty per hundred thousand per year. Notice the whole population goes underneath, not just the people who had the disease. That's what makes it a mortality rate. The share of patients who die is a different measure.

scenes.heading: 7. why the three numbers differ
scenes.speech: Side by side: two hundred new cases, five thousand five hundred living with it, and twenty deaths, all per hundred thousand. Prevalence is far bigger because type 2 diabetes usually lasts for life, so the tank keeps filling and little drains out. Pancreatic cancer is the opposite. Few people get it, but most die within a few years, so prevalence stays low. And better treatment that keeps people alive longer raises prevalence, even when incidence doesn't change.

scenes.heading: 8. counts, crude rates and age
scenes.speech: Now the hook. If a town doubles in size and its cancer cases double too, the rate hasn't changed. But a rate fixes size, not age, and most cancers are far more common in older people. Australia's population is bigger and older than thirty years ago, so the count of cancer deaths has risen, and so has the unadjusted, or crude, rate. An age-standardised rate works out what the rate would be if both years had the same age mix. On that measure, deaths have fallen.

scenes.heading: 9. collect and represent, on one denominator
scenes.speech: To collect these data, use a trusted source such as the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, and check each figure's denominator. If one value's a percentage and another's per hundred thousand, convert before you compare. Then graph them: a line graph for change over time, a bar graph for comparing groups, with the units on the axis, and the source and year in the caption. And remember, a rise in incidence can come from better screening, not only more disease.

scenes.heading: 10a. attempt one (two regions)
scenes.speech: Two exam questions. First. In 2024, Region X, with one point two million people, recorded five hundred and forty new lung cancer cases. Region Y, with three hundred thousand people, recorded one hundred and eighty. Calculate the incidence in each region per hundred thousand. Region Y's population is much older. Explain why these rates can't show which region's people are at greater risk. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 10b. feedback, item one
scenes.speech: Region X is five hundred and forty over one point two million, times a hundred thousand: forty-five per hundred thousand per year. Region Y is sixty. But lung cancer is much more common in older people, so Y's older population could explain its higher crude rate. To compare risk fairly, you'd need age-standardised rates. The classic mistake is saying X is worse because it had more cases.

scenes.heading: 10c. attempt two (a three-measure table)
scenes.speech: Second. The table shows incidence, mortality and prevalence for a non-infectious disease in Australia in 2005, 2015 and 2025, each per hundred thousand people. Describe the trend in each measure. Then explain why prevalence rose. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 10d. feedback, item two
scenes.speech: Incidence stayed steady at about sixty, so the risk of getting it didn't change. Mortality halved, from thirty to fifteen. Prevalence rose from three hundred to five hundred and forty. With fewer deaths, people live longer with the disease, so the tank fills even though the tap hasn't changed. The classic mistake is saying more people are getting the disease.

scenes.heading: 11. decision rule and handoff
scenes.speech: So for any disease data, ask three things. Is it new cases, people living with it, or deaths? Over what population and time? And is it a count, a crude rate or an age-standardised rate? Put everything on one denominator before you compare. Next, practice with new data: calculating rates and judging what they show.

scenes.heading: 12. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook (a fifteenfold rise)
scenes.speech: Between 1922 and 1947, lung cancer deaths in England and Wales rose about fifteen times. Smoking had grown, but so had tarred roads, car exhaust and factory smoke. In 1950, Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill published the first of their studies on smoking. So how do we judge an epidemiological study, and what it achieved?

scenes.heading: 2. two kinds of design
scenes.speech: Earlier, you measured disease with rates. Now we judge the studies behind them. An observational study watches what people already do, such as smoking, and compares their disease rates. In an intervention study, researchers decide who gets an exposure. In a randomised controlled trial, chance decides the groups, so other differences even out. But nobody could ethically make people smoke for decades, so the smoking evidence had to be observational.

scenes.heading: 3. the 1950 case-control study
scenes.speech: Their first study was a case-control study: it starts with the disease and looks back. They interviewed about seven hundred lung cancer patients in twenty London hospitals, each matched with a control, a patient without lung cancer, of the same sex and similar age. Then they compared smoking histories. Nearly every man with lung cancer smoked, and heavy smokers were far more common among the patients than among the controls.

scenes.heading: 4. judge the method: four steps
scenes.speech: To judge any method, use four steps: design, strength, limitation, judgement. The design is case-control. Its strength is speed, and matching meant age and sex couldn't explain the difference. Its limitation is that smoking was remembered, not recorded at the time. That opens the door to bias, a flaw in the method that pushes results one way, which more data can't cancel. The judgement: a strong association, but not yet proof of cause.

scenes.heading: 5. a third factor, and the cohort
scenes.speech: Critics asked whether a third factor, perhaps something inherited, made people both more likely to smoke and more likely to get lung cancer. A factor linked to both the exposure and the disease is a confounder. Doll and Hill's next study was a cohort study, which follows a group forward in time. In 1951, they posted a smoking questionnaire to British doctors. About forty thousand replied, and year after year, the researchers recorded which doctors died, and from what.

scenes.heading: 6. the 1954 result
scenes.speech: Doctors were easy to trace, and their causes of death were well recorded. By 1954, the lung cancer death rate rose steadily with the amount smoked: lowest in non-smokers, highest in heavy smokers. That climbing pattern is a dose-response relationship. And because smoking was recorded before anyone fell ill, the exposure clearly came first.

scenes.heading: 7. judge the cohort
scenes.speech: Now the four steps again. Design: cohort. Strengths: smoking was recorded before disease, so illness couldn't shape anyone's memory, and tens of thousands of doctors were followed for fifty years. Limitations: doctors aren't a typical population, most were men, and smoking was self-reported. It's still observational, so an unmeasured confounder can't be fully ruled out. Judgement: the strongest design that was ethical.

scenes.heading: 8. from association to cause
scenes.speech: So how did an association become a cause? Several kinds of evidence pointed the same way. The link was strong, it showed a dose-response, and exposure came first. Studies in other countries agreed. Carcinogens in smoke damage the DNA of airway cells, which gives a mechanism. And the cohort showed that doctors who quit by about thirty avoided almost all of the extra risk. Removing the exposure lowered the disease.

scenes.heading: 9. what it achieved: the benefit chain
scenes.speech: Now, what did it achieve? A benefit isn't the finding itself. It's what the finding lets people do. Picture a chain: the study identifies a risk factor that can be changed, someone makes a decision, the decision reaches people, and new data check whether disease fell. In Australia, the evidence supported warning labels, advertising bans, taxes, quit programs and plain packaging. Daily smoking fell to around one adult in ten, and men's lung cancer rates have fallen since the early 1980s.

scenes.heading: 10. how big, and its limits
scenes.speech: The benefit was large, mainly because smoking was common and could be changed. But the chain was slow: the evidence was strong by the mid-1950s, yet the biggest policies took decades. It's also unequal, because smoking is still more common in some groups. And a study asks something of its participants: time and privacy. The classic mistake is saying a study is beneficial the moment it's published.

scenes.heading: 11a. attempt one (a study to judge)
scenes.speech: Two exam questions. First. Researchers found three hundred adults with bladder cancer and six hundred without, from the same hospitals, matched for age and sex. Each was asked how often they'd used hair dye over the past twenty years. Evaluate the method used in this study. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 11b. feedback, item one
scenes.speech: It's case-control: it starts with the disease and looks back. It's quick, and matching stops age and sex explaining a difference. But hair dye use was recalled over twenty years, and people with cancer may remember differently: recall bias. So it shows an association, not a cause. The classic mistake is thinking matching removes every confounder. It only controls what was matched.

scenes.heading: 11c. attempt two (judging a benefit)
scenes.speech: Second. Studies in the 1980s and 90s linked low folate around conception with neural tube defects, where the early spinal cord doesn't close properly. From 2009, Australian bread flour had to contain folic acid. Afterwards, neural tube defects fell, most in the groups with the highest rates. Evaluate the benefit of these studies. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 11d. feedback, item two
scenes.speech: The studies found a risk factor that could be changed. Fortified flour reached people without them having to act, which matters, because the neural tube closes before many people know they're pregnant. Follow-up data showed the fall, largest in the highest-risk groups. A large benefit, though other changes may have helped. The classic mistake is saying the studies themselves prevented the defects.

scenes.heading: 12. decision rule and handoff
scenes.speech: So, for any study. To judge the method, give the design, a strength, a limitation, then decide: association or cause? To judge the benefit, follow the chain: finding, decision, action, outcome checked. Next, you'll practise rates, graphs and study judgements in exam questions.

scenes.heading: 13. key notes (quiet, about 60 seconds)
scenes.speech: Here are the key notes. Pause the video if you need more time to copy them.

scenes.heading: 1. hook
scenes.speech: Epidemiology questions in the HSC tend to ask for three things. Calculate a rate from new data, draw a graph of rates, and judge whether a study supports its claim. Here are three HSC-style questions, one of each. Pause and try each one properly, then we'll work through it together.

scenes.heading: 2a. q1-question (question 1: two regions)
scenes.speech: Question one. Two regions recorded type 2 diabetes for one year. Region P has one point two million people, with six thousand six hundred new diagnoses and three hundred deaths. Region Q has a hundred and fifty thousand people, with one thousand and fifty new diagnoses and fifty-four deaths. Calculate the incidence and mortality rates per hundred thousand for each region. Then evaluate the claim that Region P has the worse diabetes problem. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 2b. q1-calc (rates, one row at a time)
scenes.speech: Rates first, laid out as equation, substitute, solve, sense check. Incidence is new cases over the population, times a hundred thousand. For P, six thousand six hundred over one point two million, times a hundred thousand, is five hundred and fifty per hundred thousand per year. For Q, one thousand and fifty over a hundred and fifty thousand gives seven hundred. Mortality puts deaths on top. Three hundred over one point two million gives twenty-five, and fifty-four over a hundred and fifty thousand gives thirty-six. Sense check: Q is the smaller region, yet both its rates are higher.

scenes.heading: 2c. q1-claim (counts against rates, then age)
scenes.speech: Now the claim. P had more cases mainly because it has eight times as many people. Out of every hundred thousand people, Q had more new cases and more deaths, so the claim isn't supported. But before saying people in Q face a higher risk, check their ages. Type 2 diabetes becomes more common with age, so an older population would have a higher rate, even if the risk at each age were the same. Age-standardised rates, adjusted as if both regions had the same age mix, would settle it.

scenes.heading: 2d. q1-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.speech: The classic mistake is comparing raw counts. A bigger population gives more cases even when the risk is the same. Here, the region with fewer cases had the higher rates. Turn every count into a rate before you compare.

scenes.heading: 3a. q2-question (question 2: draw the rates)
scenes.speech: Question two. The table gives melanoma incidence and mortality rates in Australia, per hundred thousand people, from 1985 to 2020. Draw a line graph of both rates on one set of axes. Then describe the trend in each rate, and explain why the two rates differ so much. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 3b. q2-graph (build the graph, one stage at a time)
scenes.speech: Set up the graph before you plot anything. Year goes on the x axis, because it's the independent variable. The rate goes on the y axis, with its unit, per hundred thousand people per year. Both rates share that unit, so one axis works. Look at the years: they jump by ten, then by five at the end, so space them to scale. For the y axis, choose an even scale that fits the largest value, fifty-two: zero to sixty in tens. Plot each point, then join each set with its own ruled line, because each value is a whole year's rate, and add a key and a title. That's TAILS: title, axes, intervals, labels, scale.

scenes.heading: 3c. q2-describe (describe, then explain)
scenes.speech: Now describe and explain. Incidence rose from thirty-eight in 1985 to fifty-two in 2015, then levelled off. Mortality stayed far lower, around six, and fell to about five by 2020. They differ because most melanomas are found early, while they're still thin, and cut out, so far fewer people die than are diagnosed. Rising incidence may partly reflect more skin checks finding more cases. The recent fall in deaths fits better treatment, but this graph alone can't show that.

scenes.heading: 3d. q2-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.speech: The classic mistake is starting the y axis at thirty, to fit the incidence line. Then the mortality points fall off the graph. Choose one scale that fits every value. And space the years to scale, or the last five years look like ten.

scenes.heading: 4a. q3-question (question 3: a survey and a claim)
scenes.speech: Question three. A survey asked two thousand adults in one city whether they drink an energy drink every day, and whether they've been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Of four hundred daily drinkers, thirty-six had diabetes. Of sixteen hundred other adults, sixty-four had diabetes. A website claims that energy drinks cause type 2 diabetes. Calculate the prevalence of diabetes in each group. Then evaluate the method and the claim. Pause here to answer.

scenes.heading: 4b. q3-calc (prevalence, then name the design)
scenes.speech: Prevalence is existing cases out of the group, as a percentage. Thirty-six over four hundred is nine per cent. Sixty-four over sixteen hundred is four per cent, so diabetes was about twice as common among daily drinkers. Now name the design. Both things were measured at one moment, so it's a cross-sectional study, a snapshot. Its strength: it's quick, and it measures prevalence well.

scenes.heading: 4c. q3-evaluate (limitations, then judgement)
scenes.speech: Now the limitations. A snapshot can't show which came first, so some people may have changed their drinking after diagnosis. Daily drinkers may also differ in diet, weight, sleep or age, and any of those could be the real cause, so they're possible confounders. The answers were self-reported, online, from one city. So the data show an association, not a cause, and the claim goes too far. A stronger test is a cohort: record drinks in adults without diabetes, follow them forward, and compare who develops it, adjusting for confounders.

scenes.heading: 4d. q3-mistake (the classic mistake)
scenes.speech: The classic mistake is thinking two thousand people makes the claim proven. A big sample reduces chance, but it can't fix the design. A snapshot still can't show a cause. For that, you need the order in time, and a way to deal with confounders.

scenes.heading: 5. decision-board
scenes.speech: So, here's your first move for each type. For a rate, divide by the right population, and use the same unit for every group. For a graph, set up the axes, units and an even scale that fits every value, before you plot. For a study, name the design, then judge what it can and can't show. Next: how type 2 diabetes can be managed.

scenes.heading: 6. key-notes (reuse take: key-notes; quiet, about 60 seconds)

Treat environmental water samples as potentially contaminated and wash your hands after handling them. 📚 Core Content 2 Explain: quality depends on purpose 1 What "Water Quality" Actually Means A multi-parameter picture, not a single score Water quality is not one thing. It is a bundle of measurements that together tell chemists whether water is physically suitable, chemically balanced and biologically safe. When chemists assess water quality, they look at physical parameters such as temperature and turbidity, chemical parameters such as pH, dissolved oxygen, total dissolved solids and conductivity, and biological parameters such as coliform bacteria. No single parameter gives a complete answer. Clear water may still contain harmful dissolved ions. Neutral pH water may still be oxygen-poor. A full judgement comes from reading the measurements together. Water quality is assessed using physical parameters (temperature, turbidity), chemical parameters (pH, DO, TDS, conductivity) and biological parameters (coliform bacteria), no single measurement gives a complete picture; they must be read together. Pause, copy the highlighted definition into your book. Wrong: Clean water is water with no dissolved substances at all. Right: "Clean" water meets quality standards for specific uses, it contains acceptable levels of dissolved minerals, has safe microbial counts and is free from toxic contaminants. Pure distilled water would be unpalatable and potentially harmful. HSC language In extended responses, describe water quality as being assessed using physical, chemical and biological parameters. This shows you understand the system is multi-factor rather than single-measure. Physical signal Turbidity Suspended material and clarity, not dissolved toxins or microbes. Chemical signal pH · DO · ions Acidity, oxygen availability and dissolved load each answer different questions. Biological signal Indicator organisms Microbiological evidence requires suitable sampling and testing. Which category does coliform bacteria belong to in water quality assessment? Biological Chemical Physical Thermal 3 Represent: assemble a parameter dashboard 2 Key Water Quality Parameters What is measured and what it indicates We just saw that water quality is a multi-parameter picture. That raises a question: what exactly are those parameters, and what does each one tell a chemist? This card answers it → each parameter targets a different aspect of water condition, from temperature to microbial safety. Parameter Type What it measures Why it matters Temperature Physical Thermal condition of the water Affects dissolved oxygen and organism survival Turbidity Physical Cloudiness from suspended particles High turbidity reduces light penetration, may indicate runoff pH Chemical Acidity or alkalinity Affects chemical equilibria, toxicity and biological function Dissolved oxygen (DO) Chemical Oxygen available in water Essential for aerobic aquatic life BOD Chem/bio O₂ used by microbes to decompose organic matter High BOD suggests pollution and oxygen stress TDS Chemical Amount of dissolved ions and substances High TDS affects salinity and water suitability Conductivity Chemical Ability to conduct electricity Indirectly indicates dissolved ion concentration Coliform bacteria Biological Indicator of faecal contamination Suggests microbial safety risk Notice that some parameters are direct measurements, while others are indicators. Conductivity does not tell you exactly which ions are present, but it tells you the water contains dissolved charged species in significant amount. Conductivity is an indirect measure of dissolved ion load in water, it measures the ability of the solution to conduct electricity, which is proportional to dissolved ion concentration. Pause, copy the highlighted conductivity definition into your book. Which parameter is most directly used as an indicator of dissolved ion load in water? Conductivity Turbidity Coliform count Temperature 4 Respond: match every parameter to a method 3 How These Parameters Are Measured Field probes, chemical tests and microbiological checks We just saw the full table of water-quality parameters and what each indicates. That raises a question: how are these parameters actually measured in practice? This card answers it → each parameter has a specific measurement tool, from DO meters to microbiological culture plates. A useful parameter is not just one we can define; it is one we can measure reliably in the field or laboratory. Temperature: measured using a thermometer or temperature probe. Turbidity: measured with a turbidity meter or nephelometer. pH: measured with a pH meter or indicator method. Dissolved oxygen: measured with a DO meter or by Winkler titration. BOD: determined by comparing initial and final DO after incubation. TDS and conductivity: measured with conductivity/TDS meters. Coliform bacteria: measured using microbiological culture methods. The method chosen depends on speed, required accuracy and the question being asked. Field monitoring often favours fast probe-based measurement, while compliance testing may require more formal laboratory methods. DO can be measured by a DO meter (fast, field-based, electronic) or by Winkler titration (classical redox method); BOD is the difference between initial and final DO after 5 days at 20°C in the dark. That raises a question: once you have a measurement, how do you know whether it is acceptable or not? This card answers it → measurements only have meaning when compared against a standard such as the ADWG. A number on its own is not enough. Water-quality data become meaningful when compared with standards or acceptable ranges for human and environmental safety. The Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG) provide guidance on acceptable drinking-water quality. These guidelines are based on protecting human health as well as managing aesthetic factors such as taste, odour and appearance. For environmental monitoring, acceptable ranges can differ depending on the ecosystem and use of the water. A value that is acceptable in one context may be concerning in another, which is why chemists must interpret standards in context rather than as isolated numbers. The Australian Drinking Water Guidelines provide health-based and aesthetic guideline values for drinking-water management. They are guidance, not a universal pass/fail table for every water body. That raises a question: how do specific environmental events, like a warm discharge or agricultural runoff, actually change the parameters you measure? This card answers it → temperature and DO are inversely related, and each contamination source leaves a predictable pattern of parameter changes. A power station releases warm cooling water into a river on a hot summer afternoon, the DO probe downstream drops from 8.5 mg/L to 4.2 mg/L within three hours, while conductivity spikes with the added dissolved minerals. Two numbers changed, and each one has a specific physical and chemical cause. Water-quality interpretation becomes powerful when you can trace each parameter change back to its cause, not just record that it happened. Temperature and dissolved oxygen are inversely related : as water temperature increases, dissolved oxygen solubility decreases. This matters ecologically because warm water can place aquatic organisms under oxygen stress even before additional pollution is considered. Sample B shows several warning signs at once: higher temperature, higher turbidity, lower dissolved oxygen, higher conductivity and elevated coliform bacteria. This is exactly how real water-quality interpretation works, one concerning result matters, but a pattern of concerning results matters more. One acceptable result Supports only that parameter at that time and sampling point. Several consistent results Build a stronger physical, chemical and biological picture. Responsible conclusion State limitations, compare with purpose-specific current guidance, and recommend further testing where evidence is incomplete. Temperature and dissolved oxygen are inversely related, as water temperature increases, dissolved oxygen solubility decreases, stressing aquatic organisms even before additional pollution is present. Worked example · separating warming from pollution Problem: A river reads DO = 8.5 mg L -1 at 20 °C upstream, and DO = 4.2 mg L -1 at 28 °C downstream of a discharge. Saturation DO is 9.1 mg L -1 at 20 °C and 7.8 mg L -1 at 28 °C. How much of the fall is explained by temperature alone? 1 Find the upstream percentage saturation % sat = (8.5 / 9.1) × 100 = 93.4% Percentage saturation compares the measurement with what the water could hold at its own temperature. 2 Find the downstream percentage saturation % sat = (4.2 / 7.8) × 100 = 53.8% The same absolute reading means something different at a different temperature, which is why the raw mg L -1 value alone misleads. 3 Find the DO that warming alone would give Hold the upstream saturation: 0.934 × 7.8 = 7.3 mg L -1 expected at 28 °C If nothing but temperature had changed, the water would still be 93.4% saturated, now measured against the smaller 28 °C capacity. 4 Attribute the remainder Warming explains 8.5 - 7.3 = 1.2 mg L -1 Total fall = 8.5 - 4.2 = 4.3 mg L -1 4.3 - 1.2 = 3.1 mg L -1 unexplained by temperature About 72% of the fall needs another cause. Subtracting the two capacities instead (9.1 - 7.8 = 1.3) would assume the river started fully saturated, and it did not. 5 State what the two parameters can and cannot settle They isolate a 3.1 mg L -1 deficit that warming does not explain They do not identify its cause Flow, reaeration, salinity and photosynthesis all move DO as well. Naming the cause needs a further measurement, such as the BOD test in L07. That is exactly why quality is judged on a parameter set rather than one reading. Warm water becomes more vulnerable to oxygen stress when organic pollution or low mixing is also present. Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) The amount of O₂ consumed by microorganisms breaking down organic matter in water over 5 days at 20°C; indicator of organic pollution. Winkler titration A chemical method for measuring DO; Mn²⁺ is oxidised by dissolved O₂, then the oxidised manganese oxidises I⁻ to I₂, which is titrated with thiosulfate. DO meter An electronic probe that measures dissolved oxygen electrochemically; faster than Winkler titration but requires calibration. Temperature effect on DO DO decreases as temperature increases; warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, stressing aquatic organisms. Eutrophication and DO Excessive nutrient input → algal bloom → algae die → bacterial decomposition consumes DO → hypoxia → fish kills. DO probe technology and calibration connect to L06 (water quality parameters). The inverse temperature–DO relationship appears again in L08 (heavy metal contamination, as warmer water concentrates contaminants differently). Safety: Wear gloves, splash goggles and a lab coat. Manganese salts and alkaline iodide reagent are harmful or irritating, iodine vapour is irritating, and sulfuric acid is highly corrosive. Use ventilation, teacher supervision and intact stoppered glassware; add acid carefully, contain spills, and collect manganese/iodine reaction waste in a labelled container rather than the sink. Sodium thiosulfate is lower hazard but still requires normal laboratory care. 📚 Core Content 2 Explain: dissolved oxygen is a snapshot 1 Dissolved Oxygen as a Water-Quality Signal A direct measure of oxygen available to aquatic life Dissolved oxygen is one of the most urgent water-quality parameters because aquatic ecosystems can fail quickly when it falls too low. Dissolved oxygen (DO) is the concentration of oxygen gas dissolved in water. Fish, many invertebrates and aerobic microbes depend on it. If DO falls too low, aquatic organisms experience stress or die. DO can decrease because of higher temperature, reduced mixing, or increased biological consumption of oxygen. This is why a low DO reading is often a warning sign that the system is under chemical or biological stress. Dissolved oxygen (DO) is the concentration of O₂ dissolved in water, essential for aerobic aquatic life. DO decreases with higher temperature, reduced mixing, or increased biological consumption. A low DO reading signals chemical or biological stress. Pause, copy the highlighted DO definition into your book. Recall Lesson 6 introduced the inverse relationship between temperature and dissolved oxygen solubility. Lesson 7 extends that idea by showing how chemical and biological oxygen demand make the problem worse. What does dissolved oxygen measure? The oxygen dissolved in water and available to aquatic life The oxygen demand created by microbial decomposition over 5 days The number of bacteria in the water The amount of nitrate in the water 3 Represent: meter or Winkler titration 2 Measuring DO: DO Meter and Winkler Titration Fast instrumental reading or redox-based wet chemistry We just saw that dissolved oxygen is a critical ecological signal. That raises a question: how exactly is it measured in the field or laboratory? This card answers it → a DO meter gives speed, while the Winkler titration gives stoichiometric chemistry. A DO meter gives speed. The Winkler method gives stoichiometric chemistry. Both aim to answer the same question: how much oxygen is dissolved in the sample right now? A DO meter is a convenient field instrument that provides a rapid dissolved oxygen reading. The Winkler titration is a classical chemical method that converts the dissolved oxygen in the sample into a titre value through a chain of redox reactions. The Winkler method is especially useful in teaching because it shows that water-quality monitoring is not only about sensors, it is also about chemical transformations that can be followed quantitatively. In the Winkler titration, sodium thiosulfate does NOT titrate dissolved oxygen directly, it titrates iodine (I₂), and the amount of iodine is stoichiometrically linked to the original dissolved oxygen. Key ratio: 1 mol O₂ : 4 mol Na₂S₂O₃. Pause, copy the highlighted Winkler key ratio into your book. The Winkler method does not titrate dissolved oxygen directly. Oxygen is first trapped chemically, then converted into iodine, and finally linked to a thiosulfate titre through stoichiometry. In the Winkler method, sodium thiosulfate titrates: Iodine liberated during the redox sequence Dissolved oxygen directly Manganese ions directly Hydroxide ions produced in the sample 4 Respond: follow the Winkler stoichiometric chain 3 The Winkler Titration Chain From dissolved oxygen to iodine to thiosulfate titre We just saw that the Winkler method links DO to a thiosulfate titre through two intermediate steps. That raises a question: what are those intermediate reactions, in order? This card answers it → O₂ → MnO₂ → I₂ → thiosulfate titre, with the critical 1:4 stoichiometric shortcut. The Winkler method works because dissolved oxygen is converted into a measurable amount of iodine, and that iodine is then titrated with sodium thiosulfate. WINKLER LOGIC 1. Dissolved O 2 oxidises Mn 2+ to MnO 2 Oxygen in the sample is chemically trapped in an oxidised manganese species. 2. MnO 2 oxidises I - to I 2 The amount of iodine released depends on the oxygen originally present. 3. I 2 is titrated with Na 2 S 2 O 3 Thiosulfate volume lets the chemist calculate the original dissolved oxygen. Stoichiometric shortcut: 1 mol O 2 : 4 mol Na 2 S 2 O 3 This is the critical ratio for HSC calculations. Winkler chain: O₂ oxidises Mn²⁺ to MnO₂ → MnO₂ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ → I₂ is titrated with Na₂S₂O₃. HSC shortcut: 1 mol O₂ : 4 mol Na₂S₂O₃. Thiosulfate titrates iodine, NOT oxygen directly. 1 · Titre n(S₂O₃²⁻) = cV 2 · Ratio n(O₂) = n(S₂O₃²⁻) / 4 3 · Mass m(O₂) = n × 32.00 4 · Concentration Convert sample result to mg L⁻¹ Pause, copy the highlighted Winkler chain into your book. That raises a question: what if the real problem is not the oxygen right now, but the oxygen that will be consumed over the next five days? This card answers it → BOD₅ measures that future oxygen demand, making it a forecast rather than a snapshot. Dissolved oxygen gives a snapshot. BOD gives a forecast of oxygen stress caused by biodegradable organic matter. Biochemical Oxygen Demand , usually measured as BOD 5 , is the amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms as they decompose organic matter over five days at 20°C in the dark. BOD 5 REFERENCE BOD 5 = initial DO − final DO Measured after 5 days at 20°C in the dark < 2 mg L -1 = clean water Low biochemical oxygen demand 2–8 mg L -1 = moderate pollution Noticeable oxygen demand from decomposing matter > 8 mg L -1 = heavy pollution High oxygen demand and major ecological concern BOD₅ = initial DO − final DO after five days at 20°C in the dark. BOD measures oxygen consumed by microbial decomposition, not oxygen currently present. Higher BOD indicates greater biodegradable organic load; interpret categories against the stated course or monitoring context rather than as universal legal thresholds. Pause, copy the highlighted BOD formula and thresholds into your book. Misconception "BOD measures how much oxygen is in the water." Not quite. BOD measures how much oxygen is used up by microbial decomposition. A high BOD means more pollution pressure, not more oxygen availability. What does a BOD₅ value above 8 mg L⁻¹ indicate? Heavy pollution and high oxygen demand Very clean water No microbial activity High dissolved oxygen availability 6 Feedback: BOD is not a universal toxicity test 5 Eutrophication and Oxygen Depletion Why nutrient-rich water can end in fish kill We just saw that high BOD signals a heavy organic load consuming oxygen. That raises a question: where does that organic load come from in a natural river, and how does it turn into a fish kill? This card answers it → eutrophication is the six-step chain from excess nutrients to aquatic death, driven by microbial decomposition raising the BOD. A green-tinted river on a warm Monday morning looks like a minor aesthetic problem. By Friday, after the algal bloom begins to die and bacteria surge to decompose the biomass, the dissolved oxygen has collapsed below 1 mg/L and fish are surfacing for air. The danger of eutrophication is not the bloom itself but the oxygen crash that follows it. Excess nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates enter the water. Algal growth increases rapidly, producing a bloom. Light penetration falls and submerged plants die. Dead algae and plants are decomposed by microorganisms. Microbial respiration raises oxygen demand (high BOD). Dissolved oxygen falls, causing hypoxia and possible fish kill. This is why BOD and DO together are so useful: one shows how much oxygen is available, and the other shows how strongly the system is likely to consume it. Critical limitation: BOD responds mainly to biodegradable organic matter under the test conditions. A low BOD does not prove water is safe because toxic metals, persistent organic pollutants, pathogens or other non-biodegradable hazards may still be present. Eutrophication sequence: excess nutrients → algal bloom → light loss + plant death → microbial decomposition → high BOD → low DO → hypoxia → fish kill. DO = snapshot of oxygen now; BOD = forecast of future oxygen demand. Pause, copy the highlighted eutrophication chain into your book. Show All Answers MC Answers: 1-A, 2-D, 3-B, 4-C, 5-A Activity 1: (1) n(thiosulfate) = 0.0200 × 0.00650 = 1.30 × 10⁻⁴ mol. n(O₂) = 1.30 × 10⁻⁴ / 4 = 3.25 × 10⁻⁵ mol. m(O₂) = 3.25 × 10⁻⁵ × 32.00 = 1.04 × 10⁻³ g = 1.04 mg in 100.0 mL. DO = 10.4 mg L⁻¹. (2) The thiosulfate titrates iodine, and the amount of iodine is stoichiometrically related to the original dissolved oxygen through the Winkler redox chain. Activity 2: (1) BOD₅ = 9.0 − 7.6 = 1.4 mg L⁻¹, clean water. (2) BOD₅ 9.5 mg L⁻¹ → heavy pollution, serious oxygen demand and likely ecological stress. (3) Excess nutrients → algal bloom → algae die → microbial decomposition → oxygen demand rises → dissolved oxygen falls → hypoxia → fish kill. Q1 (4 marks): Dissolved oxygen first oxidises Mn²⁺ to MnO₂. The oxidised manganese then oxidises I⁻ to I₂. That iodine is titrated with sodium thiosulfate. Because the amount of iodine depends on the oxygen originally present, the thiosulfate titre can be converted stoichiometrically to dissolved oxygen. Key HSC ratio: 1 mol O₂ to 4 mol Na₂S₂O₃. Q2 (4 marks): DO measures how much oxygen is currently dissolved and available for aquatic life. BOD₅ measures how much oxygen microorganisms consume over 5 days while decomposing organic matter. After an algal bloom, DO shows the immediate oxygen status, while BOD₅ indicates how strongly the system will keep consuming oxygen. Together they give both a snapshot and a forecast of oxygen stress. Q3 (5 marks): BOD₅ is useful because it indicates the biodegradable organic load by measuring oxygen consumed during microbial decomposition. After an algal bloom this is valuable because dead algae can drive strong oxygen demand and threaten aquatic life. A limitation is that BOD₅ alone does not show the current dissolved oxygen level at sampling, so it cannot describe the immediate river condition. It should be interpreted alongside DO and other water-quality data. Overall, BOD₅ is a strong pollution indicator but most useful as part of a broader assessment. Return to the Hawkesbury River Case Return to the 2007 Hawkesbury-Nepean cyanobacteria bloom. Now that you understand DO and BOD 5 , explain the analytical sequence that NSW DPI scientists followed. Why did the initial DO reading of 5.5 mg/L give false reassurance, and why did the BOD 5 of 9.2 mg/L O₂/L provide the critical warning instead? How does microbial decomposition of dead algal biomass actually drive the DO crash that kills fish days after the bloom peaks? Write one sentence distinguishing clearly between DO (instantaneous measurement) and BOD 5 (predictive measurement) as used by river-monitoring scientists. ✓ Review: check what actually stuck Quick Quiz 🏆 Review What is the formula for BOD₅, and what does a higher result indicate? Show answer BOD₅ = initial DO − final DO after five days at 20°C in the dark. A higher result indicates greater oxygen consumption by microbial decomposition and therefore greater biodegradable organic load; categories depend on the stated monitoring context. Give the stoichiometric shortcut for the Winkler titration. Show answer 1 mol O₂ : 4 mol Na₂S₂O₃. Thiosulfate titrates iodine (not oxygen directly), and the iodine amount is stoichiometrically linked to the original dissolved oxygen. What is the difference between dissolved oxygen and BOD₅? Show answer Dissolved oxygen measures the oxygen currently present and available to aquatic life (snapshot). BOD₅ measures how much oxygen microbes consume over 5 days while decomposing organic matter (forecast of future oxygen demand). List the 6 steps in the eutrophication sequence. Show answer 1. Excess nutrients enter the water. 2. Algal bloom develops. 3. Light penetration falls; submerged plants die. 4. Dead algae and plants are decomposed by microbes. 5. Microbial respiration raises oxygen demand (BOD rises). 6. Dissolved oxygen falls → hypoxia → fish kill. What does a DO meter measure, and what is one advantage over the Winkler titration? Show answer A DO meter measures dissolved oxygen electrochemically via a probe. Advantage: it is faster and more suitable for field use than the multi-step Winkler wet-chemistry method.
